name: Runtimely 2026.11.0
description:
One engine, every app

## New

- Runtimely: a launcher that runs every app against one Electron engine, instead of a Chromium copy per app.
- Runtimely stays resident: closing the window leaves it running in the tray, and a second launch brings the
  window up — restored and focused — rather than starting a second copy.
- A plugin that fails to load stops the launch and says why in Runtimely's own start log, rather than leaving a
  half-broken app on screen.
- Runtimely: its own start is drawn in a black window reading "Runtimely {percent}%" above a copyable log of
  what is loading, with minimise and close; a plugin that cannot load stops the boot with the reason in that
  log, and the window stays until it is closed.
- Runtimely's own icon, tray icon and executable icon all come from one master image.
- Library: a list of installed apps — each row carrying the app's name, author, description, version, and the
  app's own icon or the letter its name computes.
- Library: an app with no icon is one theme placeholder square with the first letter of its name; an icon that
  loads takes its background colour from the image instead.
- Library: one control per row starts an app, and then reads Running while it is up.
- Library: a press on that control shows a window while the app starts — the app's name, the step it has
  reached, and a bar that fills as the app's own window appears, held a moment at 100%.
- Library: the tray icon opens the library, the menu carries the way out, and a running app is offered there.
- Library: a plus control opens the install dialog — an online tab listing a catalogue address, and a local tab
  that reads dropped or chosen `.rtp` packages.
- Library: an app already at the catalogue's version offers Reinstall rather than a dead control, so its own
  package can be put back.
- Library: an empty library explains itself in words rather than showing nothing.
- Library: a details dialog per app, with a tab strip — Info for identity, version and description, Config for
  the app's own settings, and Permissions for the answers that app has been given, each with a reset that makes
  Runtimely ask again.
- Config: an app's own theme variant, theme and language, each the same control Runtimely's settings draw, each
  leading with Follow Runtimely, and each with its own reset.
- Config: a button that writes a desktop shortcut for that app, named after the app and carrying its own icon,
  and saying what its last press did.
- Settings: Runtimely's own theme, variant, language, catalogue address and whether to close the library on a
  launch — every setting written as it changes and each with its own reset, and a write that cannot be made
  puts the field back to the value it held and says why.
- About: Runtimely's version, and each credit as a row with its licence and an opaque mark whose background is
  sampled from the image, opening its own address in your browser.
- Overlay: what is running, with the windows each app has open and a control that ends it.
- Apps: a package installs only after every file in it is checked, so nothing can escape the folder it belongs
  in, take a name Windows reserves, or arrive under one that is not the name it shipped with.
- Apps: an app runs in its own process, started the same way from a shortcut, from a package, or from a line
  handed to a Runtimely that is already up — and starting one that is already running brings it up rather than
  starting it twice.
- Apps: an app can keep running with no window open, be told when something about it changes, and end when it
  has nothing left on screen.
- Apps: an app's pages and windows follow that app's own theme, variant and language, which can differ from
  Runtimely's.
- Apps: an app's own window can close itself and nothing else — every other call it could make is refused.
- Apps: Runtimely stops every running app when it quits.
- Permissions: an app that wants one asks, and the prompt is the gate — default deny, Runtimely's own theme
  and language, and the name of the app that is asking.
- Permissions: eight can be asked — microphone, camera, screen capture, clipboard, notifications, files, open
  links and idle time.
- Permissions: Remember my choice writes the answer to the app's own record; an unticked Accept is kept for
  that run only, and an unticked Deny — or the close control, which reads Deny and close — asks again next time.
- Permissions: one prompt per app at a time, so a second request waits rather than deciding two things with
  one press, and a permission ends with the app's run.
- Themes: a theme is a set of tokens with a light and a dark value each, reloaded when a user's file changes;
  the base values and one named theme, Horizon, ship with it, and every colour pair in both variants meets
  contrast.
- Themes: a theme file with a value that would break out of its own declaration, or one of the wrong shape for
  its token, is refused with the base value standing.
- Themes: themes carry a background image and their own durations, and the percent figure is drawn as the bar
  itself, dark enough to read.
- Themes: the editor's Add, Preview, Rename and Delete buttons stay above the overrides, and a theme can be
  renamed or deleted from its own confirmation.
- Themes: an override is edited with a native colour control, a length's unit comes from the same dropdown as
  every other control, and the background image is chosen from a file button that copies it into the plugin's
  own data.
- Themes: every variable in the overrides and the add list says what it changes, and the preview is one compact
  sample rather than a gallery of every token.
- Themes: the add list groups variables under headings that start closed and open on a press, so a long token
  list begins with its categories rather than every variable at once.
- Languages: a language can be added, every language is named in its own words, and the language dropdown
  shows each one with its own bar and a percentage label centred on it, set apart from the name.
- Languages: a word a language is missing shows as its own key, so the gap reads as the path still owed.
- Dialogs: scrolling rows keep the same inset on both sides and above and below their content, with room for
  the bar without reserving an empty column, and a theme dialog's action buttons keep their distance from the
  text above.
- Icons: every icon is Phosphor, in regular, bold and fill.
- Windows: a window shows only the document its own plugin was given — it cannot navigate away, open another
  window, or reach a file outside that folder.
- Overlay: each app's prompt is a window of its own, so two apps asking at once are two prompts, and the panel
  can be dragged by its body without pressing its controls.
- Tray: each app's and plugin's rows sit in their own submenu, named in the language in effect.
- Tray: the library opens from its own icon and adds no row to the menu, and the apps manager's row reads Open.
- Dialogs: a card is as wide as what it holds, its tab strip scrolls sideways rather than wrapping to a second
  line, and Escape, the close control and the backdrop do the same thing in every dialog.
- Dropdowns: the list is as wide as its widest item, each item is as tall as the control it came from, and the
  rows are spaced.
- Errors: messages say what actually went wrong and what to do about it.
- Updater: the release's version is read first, and nothing is downloaded when it is not newer. A release is
  read as untrusted — a page where a version was expected is not a version, and a redirect from https to http
  is refused.
- Updater: its own window shows the version line, the release notes and an Update button, and the button fills
  as a progress bar for the download. Notes are read from the field a feed really fills, with markup stripped,
  escaped references decoded and line breaks kept, drawn at reading size in a window grown to fit.
- Updater: the changes are drawn in the changelog's own sections — New, Improvements, Fixes and Misc — with the
  release's lead line above them, and a release written as plain prose still reads as one block.
- Updater: Check now checks whatever the startup switch says, and a version that is already current opens a
  window saying so rather than showing a changelog.
- Updater: the pack is staged for the next launch to swap in, never restarted into before the swap, and an
  update can carry a new updater — a pack that brings none falls back to the one inside the app.

commit.title: Leave the tray choice to the app that owns it
commit.message:
Leave the tray choice to the app that owns it

1) Revert the host's minimize-to-tray setting and the library's exit on close
2) Let an app change whether its window hides on close, and tell it when a window closes
3) Keep the host's window behavior generic, so no app's tray policy lives in the launcher
